title: Btrfs
text:
The core data structure of Btrfsthe copy-on-write B-treewas originally proposed by IBM researcher Ohad Rodeh at a USENIX conference in 2007.[1] Chris Mason, an engineer working on ReiserFS for SUSE at the time, joined Oracle later that year and began work on a new file system based on B-trees.[2]

In 2008, the principal developer of the ext3 and ext4 file systems, Theodore Ts'o, stated that although ext4 has improved features, it is not a major advance; it uses old technology and is a stop-gap. Ts'o said that Btrfs is the better direction because "it offers improvements in scalability, reliability, and ease of management".[3] Btrfs also has "a number of the same design ideas that reiser3/4 had".[4]

Btrfs 1.0, with finalized on-disk format, was originally slated for a late-2008 release,[5] and was finally accepted into the Linux kernel mainline in 2009.[6] Several Linux distributions began offering Btrfs as an experimental choice of root file system during installation.[7,8,9]

In July 2011, Btrfs automatic defragmentation and scrubbing features were merged into version 3.0 of the Linux kernel mainline.[10] Besides Mason at Oracle, Miao Xie at Fujitsu contributed performance improvements.[11] In June 2012, Mason left Oracle for Fusion-io, which he left a year later with Josef Bacik to join Facebook. While at both companies, Mason continued his work on Btrfs.[12,2]

In 2012, two Linux distributions moved Btrfs from experimental to production or supported status: Oracle Linux in March,[13] followed by SUSE Linux Enterprise in August.[14]

In 2015, Btrfs was adopted as the default file system for SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLE) 12.[15]

In August 2017, Red Hat announced in the release notes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 7.4 that it no longer planned to move Btrfs to a fully supported feature (it's been included as a "technology preview" since RHEL 6 beta) noting that it would remain available in the RHEL 7 release series.[16] Btrfs was removed from RHEL 8 in May 2019.[17] RHEL moved from ext4 in RHEL 6 to XFS in RHEL 7.[18]

In 2020, Btrfs was selected as the default file system for Fedora 33 for desktop variants.[19]
